intro: In English, people often use one word, kung fu, for every Chinese martial art. In China the picture is much wider. There are northern and southern systems, family styles named for villages and teachers, temple stories, national programs, and a modern sport with two separate rule books.

In this unit you will visit real places: the Shaolin Monastery in Henan, Chen Village, a Shanghai club founded in 1910 and a national institute in Nanjing. You will also meet the films that made some of these names famous around the world, from Hong Kong studios to American television.

By the end, you will be able to name the words Chinese speakers use for martial arts. You will tell a legend from a record, and taolu from sanda. You will also be able to check a school's name by asking for its place, its teachers, its governing body and its papers.
bigQuestion: How do we find the real places, people and rule books behind the one English word kung fu?

title: China Is Not One Kung Fu

chapters.title: Many Systems
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do historians say that China has many martial arts instead of one thing called kung fu?

story.title: Two Plans for One Building
story.kicker: One sports hall holds a carpet for routines and a raised platform for bouts.
paragraphs: A national wushu meet fills a large sports hall in China. On one side lies a flat carpet marked with a rectangle. On the other side stands a square platform raised above the floor. Both spaces belong to the same sport body, the Chinese Wushu Association, founded in 1958.

On the carpet, one athlete at a time performs a set routine called a taolu. No one faces an opponent. A panel of judges sits along the edge and gives each routine a score. Some routines use a sword, a staff or a spear. Others use no equipment at all.

On the platform, two athletes in padded gear meet in timed rounds. This contest is called sanda. A referee stands with them, and judges keep points. An athlete can lose points or a round by leaving the platform.

A visitor who only knows the English word kung fu might think this is one art. It is not. The hall holds two separate codes. Behind them stand hundreds of older family and village systems. This chapter maps some of them.
story.think: Why might one sports body run two very different contests in the same building?

lessons.title: Words for the Arts
lessons.mainIdea: Chinese uses several words for martial arts, and each one comes from a different time and purpose.
reading: In Mandarin Chinese, the common word for martial arts is *wushu*. It joins wu, meaning military or martial, with shu, meaning art or skill. The word is old. Today it is also the official name of a modern sport run by national and world federations.

The English word kung fu comes from *gongfu*. In Chinese, gongfu means skill gained through long effort and time. A cook or a calligrapher can have gongfu. The spelling kung fu follows an older way of writing Chinese sounds in Latin letters.

In the 1920s and 1930s, China's Republican government used a third word, *guoshu*. It means national art. Leaders chose it to link martial arts with the nation and public health. Each word points to a different chapter of history.

words.d: the Mandarin word for martial arts; also the name of a modern sport with judged routines and bouts
a Chinese word for skill built through long effort; the source of the English word kung fu
national art; the name China's Republican government gave martial arts in the 1920s and 1930s

lessons.title: South Fist, North Leg
lessons.mainIdea: A Chinese saying sorts many arts into northern and southern families, though the real map is more mixed.
reading: China is a large country with many regions and languages. Martial arts grew up in many local places. An old Chinese saying groups them roughly: *nanquan beitui*. It means southern fists, northern legs.

Northern systems grew in provinces such as Hebei, Shandong and Henan. Names include Chaquan and Bajiquan. Southern systems grew in Guangdong and Fujian. Names include Hung Gar, Choy Li Fut and Wing Chun. Many southern names reached the world in Cantonese spelling, through Hong Kong and emigrants.

The saying is a rough label, not a rule. Teachers moved between provinces, and families traded ideas. Modern wushu keeps the old split in its events. It has a Changquan event, for long fist, and a *Nanquan* event, for southern fist.

words.d: a Chinese saying, southern fists, northern legs, that roughly sorts arts by region
southern fist; a modern wushu event based on arts from southern China

lessons.title: A Village and a Family Name
lessons.mainIdea: Many Chinese arts are tied to a family or village line, such as taijiquan from Chen Village in Henan.
reading: Chenjiagou, or *Chen Village*, lies in Henan Province. The Chen family there kept a martial art for generations. Historians link the earliest records of *taijiquan* to this village in the 1600s and 1700s.

In the 1800s, Yang Luchan studied in Chen Village. He later taught in Beijing, where his students included people close to the imperial court. His teaching grew into Yang style. Other teachers founded Wu, Sun and Hao styles. Each style carries a family name.

Styles named for families show how arts spread: teacher to student, one line at a time. In 2020, UNESCO added taijiquan to its list of the *intangible cultural heritage* of humanity. The listing honored a living practice kept by communities, not one single school.

words.d: Chenjiagou, a village in Henan Province linked to the earliest records of taijiquan
a Chinese martial art with several family styles, practiced today by millions for health and sport
a living practice, like a craft, song or art, that UNESCO lists as worth protecting

lessons.title: The Shaolin Monastery
lessons.mainIdea: Shaolin is a real Buddhist monastery in Henan, founded in 495 CE, with records of monks who fought.
reading: The *Shaolin Monastery* stands on Mount Song in Henan Province. Emperor Xiaowen of the Northern Wei dynasty had it built in 495 CE. It was made for an Indian monk named Batuo. It is a Buddhist temple first, a home for monks and their teaching.

A stone tablet, or *stele*, at the temple dates from 728 CE. It records that Shaolin monks helped Li Shimin in 621 CE. Li Shimin later became Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty. In return, the monastery received land.

Later records from the Ming dynasty, in the 1500s, describe Shaolin monks fighting coastal raiders with staffs. In 1928 a warlord's army burned much of the temple. In 2010 UNESCO listed Shaolin within the Historic Monuments of Dengfeng as a World Heritage site.

words.d: a Buddhist monastery on Mount Song in Henan, China, founded in 495 CE
a carved stone slab with writing, set up to record an event

check.why: The Shaolin Monastery stands on Mount Song in Henan Province, China.

check.q: What is the Shaolin Monastery first of all?

lessons.title: The Bodhidharma Legend
lessons.mainIdea: The story that Bodhidharma taught fighting at Shaolin is a legend; historians trace it to a text from the 1600s.
reading: *Bodhidharma* was a Buddhist monk from India or Central Asia. Chinese Buddhist writings say he came to China in the 400s or 500s. Chan Buddhism, called Zen in Japan, honors him as a founder. Early writings about him describe meditation, not fighting.

A popular *legend* says Bodhidharma taught the Shaolin monks exercises that became their martial art. The story is linked to a book called the *Yijin Jing*, or Sinew-Changing Classic. Its preface claims an ancient origin. Historians date the text to the early 1600s.

In the 1930s the Chinese historian Tang Hao studied these claims. He argued that the Bodhidharma story did not match the older records. Later scholars, such as Meir Shahar, agree. The legend is still told in many schools, so historians label it as a story.

words.d: a Buddhist monk honored as a founder of Chan (Zen) Buddhism; legends link him to Shaolin fighting
a story passed down about the past that records cannot prove
the Sinew-Changing Classic, an exercise text historians date to the early 1600s

look.title: A Historian on the Legend
look.text: The Sinew-Changing Classic was written in the early 1600s, not in Bodhidharma's time. Its claim of an ancient Indian origin is a later invention that made the text seem more important.
look.cite: Meir Shahar, The Shaolin Monastery: History, Religion, and the Chinese Martial Arts (2008)
look.prompt: Why might a writer in the 1600s give an exercise book a famous old author?

check.q: When do historians date the Yijin Jing?
check.why: Historians date the Sinew-Changing Classic to the early 1600s, long after Bodhidharma.

check.q: Who studied the Bodhidharma claims in the 1930s?

lessons.title: Mountains and Founders
lessons.mainIdea: Stories that one person invented an art on a mountain are legends that sit beside the real history of temples.
reading: The *Wudang Mountains* are in Hubei Province. They are home to many Daoist temples. Ming emperors paid for large buildings there in the 1400s. In 1994 UNESCO listed the Ancient Building Complex in the Wudang Mountains as a World Heritage site.

A legend says a Daoist named Zhang Sanfeng invented taijiquan at Wudang after watching animals. Records that tie him to taijiquan appear only centuries later. Historians such as Tang Hao found no early evidence for the claim.

Founding stories like this are common. They give a school an old and famous *origin*. Some writers set a Wudang family of arts against a Shaolin family, as if one were Daoist and one Buddhist. Historians treat that pairing as a later way of sorting, not an ancient fact.

words.d: mountains in Hubei, China, known for Daoist temples built with support from Ming emperors
the beginning of something; where and how it started

look.title: Two Kinds of Evidence
look.text: Evidence A: a temple hall at Wudang built with money from a Ming emperor in the 1400s, still standing. Evidence B: a school pamphlet that says Zhang Sanfeng invented its art after watching a bird and a snake.
look.prompt: Which piece of evidence can a historian date and check? What would you need to trust the other one?

lessons.title: Jingwu in Shanghai
lessons.mainIdea: The Jingwu Athletic Association, founded in Shanghai in 1910, taught many styles in one public club.
reading: In 1910 a group in Shanghai founded the *Jingwu Athletic Association*. It is also spelled Chin Woo. The martial artist Huo Yuanjia was linked to its start. He died in 1910, the year it opened.

Older teaching often happened inside a family or a small circle of students. Jingwu was different. It was a public *association*, a club with members, officers and a written purpose. It taught several northern and southern styles in one place, along with sports and music.

Jingwu opened branches in other Chinese cities. By the 1920s it also had branches in Southeast Asia, where many Chinese families had moved. Its model made martial arts look like a modern club activity, open to people outside one teacher's family.

words.d: a public martial arts club founded in Shanghai in 1910, also spelled Chin Woo
a club or group with members, leaders and written goals

lessons.title: The Central Guoshu Institute
lessons.mainIdea: In 1928 the Nationalist government founded the Central Guoshu Institute in Nanjing to make martial arts a national program.
reading: In 1928 China's Nationalist government set up the *Central Guoshu Institute* in Nanjing, then the capital. Its leader was Zhang Zhijiang, a general. Its goal was to make martial arts a national program for health and defense.

The institute trained teachers and held national examinations, the first in 1928. Provinces and counties opened their own guoshu halls. Teachers from rival styles were asked to work under one national roof. This was a new idea after centuries of local teaching.

In 1936 China sent a team to show martial arts at the Berlin Olympic Games. It was a *demonstration*, not a medal event. The program was cut short when Japan's full-scale invasion of China began in 1937 and war spread.

words.d: a national martial arts school the Nationalist government founded in Nanjing in 1928
a show of a sport or art for an audience, with no medals given

check.why: General Zhang Zhijiang led the Central Guoshu Institute in Nanjing.

lessons.title: Taolu as a Judged Routine
lessons.mainIdea: After 1949 China turned many styles into standard taolu routines that judges score like a performance.
reading: After the People's Republic of China was founded in 1949, the state organized sport through national bodies. The *Chinese Wushu Association* was founded in 1958. Committees wrote standard routines drawn from many older styles, so every athlete could be judged on the same set.

A *taolu* is a set routine performed alone. It is judged a bit like gymnastics or figure skating. Under world federation rules, separate judges score the quality of movement, the overall performance and the degree of difficulty.

Taolu events carry old names. Changquan draws on northern styles, Nanquan on southern ones, and Taijiquan on the family styles. Weapon events include the broadsword, straight sword, staff and spear. A judged event rewards a clean performance, not a win over a partner.

words.d: China's national governing body for wushu, founded in 1958
a set routine performed alone and scored by judges in modern wushu

look.title: A Judge's Sheet
look.text: A judge's sheet has three boxes. Box one is for how well the moves are done. Box two is for rhythm, spirit and the routine as a whole. Box three is for the hard elements the athlete includes. There is no box for an opponent.
look.prompt: What other sports are judged this way? What makes taolu different from a bout?

check.why: A taolu is a set routine performed alone and judged.

check.q: Which sport is judged most like taolu?
check.why: Like figure skating, taolu is scored by judges on quality, performance and difficulty.

lessons.title: Sanda as Another Code
lessons.mainIdea: Sanda is a separate wushu code: a timed bout between two athletes on a raised platform.
reading: *Sanda*, also called sanshou, means free fighting. China developed it as a modern contest sport in the late 1970s and 1980s, with national rules and national meets. It is part of wushu, but it follows its own rule book.

Sanda bouts take place on a raised square platform called a *leitai*. The name comes from older public challenge stages. Athletes wear gloves, headgear and body protectors, and they are sorted into weight classes. Referees and judges award points, and leaving the platform costs points.

Taolu and sanda share a governing body but not a rule book. One is judged like a performance. The other is scored like boxing or wrestling. Knowing which code is in use tells you what an athlete is trying to do.

words.d: free fighting; a modern wushu bout sport, also called sanshou
the raised square platform used for sanda bouts, named after older challenge stages

look.text: Rule book A, taolu: one athlete, a carpet, a set routine, a panel of judges, a score out of ten. Rule book B, sanda: two athletes, a raised platform, gloves and headgear, weight classes, timed rounds, points and a winner.

check.q: How do taolu and sanda differ?

check.why: Both are wushu, but taolu is judged as a solo routine and sanda is scored as a contest between two athletes.

lessons.title: Wushu Goes Worldwide
lessons.mainIdea: Since 1990 a world federation has run wushu contests, and the English word kung fu hides this whole map.
reading: The *International Wushu Federation* was founded in 1990. Wushu joined the Asian Games in Beijing that same year. The first World Wushu Championships were held in Beijing in 1991, with athletes from many countries.

At the 2008 Beijing Olympics, a wushu tournament was held with the organizers' approval, but it was not an official Olympic medal sport. The IOC later chose wushu for the 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, Senegal.

In English, one word, kung fu, often covers all of this. It can mean a village art, a family style, a temple story, a sport routine or a movie scene. Using one word this way can *flatten* the map. Historians bring the map back by naming the place, the teaching line and the rule book.

words.d: the world governing body for wushu, founded in 1990
to press many different things into one label so their differences disappear

chapters.title: Name the Room Not the Movie
chapters.bigQuestion: How can we tell what a real school, person or style was, when films have told the story louder?

story.title: A Poster and a Charter
story.kicker: A film poster and a club's founding papers use the same name in different ways.
paragraphs: A library display holds two items side by side. The first is a poster for Fist of Fury, a Hong Kong film from 1972. It stars Bruce Lee. The poster shows the name of a real Shanghai club, Jingwu, in large letters.

The second item is a copy of papers about that same club. They record that the Jingwu Athletic Association was founded in Shanghai in 1910. They list members, officers and the styles taught. They describe a public club for exercise and training.

The film tells a story set around the club after Huo Yuanjia's death. Its hero, Chen Zhen, is a character written for the screen. The papers describe the club's real founding and the people who ran it.

Both items use the word Jingwu. One is a story made to move an audience. The other is a record made to run an institution. A historian reads each one for what it can honestly show, and checks names and dates against the club's own papers.
story.think: If you only saw the poster, what might you believe about Jingwu that the papers would change?

lessons.title: Wong Fei-hung the Doctor
lessons.mainIdea: Wong Fei-hung was a real doctor and teacher in Guangdong, and films turned him into a legend.
reading: Wong Fei-hung lived from 1847 to 1924 in Guangdong Province, in southern China. He learned the Hung Gar style from his father, Wong Kei-ying. He practiced traditional Chinese medicine and ran a clinic called Po Chi Lam in Foshan.

Starting in 1949, Hong Kong studios made a long series of films about him. The actor Kwan Tak-hing played him in dozens of them. In 1991 director Tsui Hark made Once Upon a Time in China, with Jet Li as Wong. Each film invented new adventures.

A *biography* is a true account of a person's life, based on records. A *folk hero* is a real or imagined person whose story grows as people retell it. Wong Fei-hung is both. Historians separate the doctor in Foshan from the hero on the screen.

words.d: a true account of a person's life, built from records
a person whose story grows larger as people retell it in songs, books or films

lessons.title: Huo Yuanjia and a Screen Student
lessons.mainIdea: Huo Yuanjia was a real martial artist linked to Jingwu; his famous film student Chen Zhen was invented.
reading: Huo Yuanjia was a martial artist from Tianjin, in northern China. He is linked to the founding of the Jingwu Athletic Association in Shanghai. He died in 1910. Stories about him say he took on foreign strongmen who issued public challenges.

In 1972 Fist of Fury, made by Golden Harvest in Hong Kong, told a story set after his death. Bruce Lee played Chen Zhen, a student who seeks justice. Chen Zhen is a *fictional* character, created for the film. The film shows Japanese characters mocking the Chinese as weak.

The film spoke to anger about foreign power in China in the early 1900s. It was made for audiences in Hong Kong, then a British colony, and across Asia. In 2006 Jet Li starred in Fearless, another film about Huo. It too mixed record and invention.

words.d: made up for a story; not a real person or event
a place ruled by a distant country; Hong Kong was a British colony until 1997

look.title: Record or Screen?

look.prompt: Which of the four facts is about a fictional person? Which are about real records?

check.why: Hong Kong was a British colony until 1997.

lessons.title: Ip Man in Hong Kong
lessons.mainIdea: Ip Man taught Wing Chun in Hong Kong from the 1950s; films about him came decades after his death.
reading: Ip Man was born in Foshan, Guangdong, in 1893. He learned Wing Chun there. After 1949 he moved to Hong Kong, where he began teaching Wing Chun in the early 1950s. He died in Hong Kong in 1972.

In Hong Kong, Ip Man taught in rented rooms and rooftops, and his students opened schools of their own. One of his students was a teenager named Bruce Lee. Through students who moved abroad, Ip Man's *lineage* reached Europe, North America and Australia.

In 2008 the film Ip Man, starring Donnie Yen, made him famous to millions who had never heard of him. It added invented fights and events. Sequels followed. Many new students came to Wing Chun schools because of the films, and teachers had to explain what was history and what was screen story.

words.d: a southern Chinese martial art from Guangdong, taught in Hong Kong by Ip Man and his students
a line of teachers and students that passes an art from one generation to the next

lessons.title: Bruce Lee Between School and Screen
lessons.mainIdea: Bruce Lee ran real schools in the United States and named his own approach Jeet Kune Do in 1967.
reading: Bruce Lee was born in San Francisco in 1940 and grew up in Hong Kong. He studied Wing Chun with Ip Man. In 1959 he moved to the United States. In Seattle he opened a school and called his teaching Jun Fan Gung Fu. He later taught in Oakland and Los Angeles.

Lee taught students who were not Chinese, at a time when some teachers in Chinatowns taught only Chinese students. In 1967 he gave his own approach a name: *Jeet Kune Do*. The name means way of the intercepting fist in Cantonese. He called it a way of thinking about fighting rather than a fixed style.

His films The Big Boss (1971), Fist of Fury (1972) and Enter the Dragon (1973) made him a world star. He died in Hong Kong in July 1973, at age 32, just before Enter the Dragon opened. Enter the Dragon was made by Warner Bros. with Golden Harvest, a Hong Kong studio.

words.d: the name Bruce Lee gave his approach in 1967; Cantonese for way of the intercepting fist
a neighborhood in a city outside China where many Chinese families live and run businesses

lessons.title: Studios and Shaolin Films
lessons.mainIdea: Hong Kong studios made Shaolin a famous film setting, and a 1982 film sent crowds of visitors to the real temple.
reading: In the 1960s and 1970s, Hong Kong studios such as Shaw Brothers made many martial arts films. A *genre* is a type of film with familiar settings and stories. Shaolin became one of the genre's favorite settings. The 36th Chamber of Shaolin, from Shaw Brothers in 1978, showed a hero training through many halls.

Those halls were a film set. The real temple's records do not list thirty-six chambers. Films borrowed the temple's name and its legends, then invented new ones. Audiences in Hong Kong, Southeast Asia and later the West came to picture Shaolin through these sets.

In 1982 the film Shaolin Temple, starring a young Jet Li, was shot partly at the real monastery in Henan. It was a huge hit in China. Visitors poured into Dengfeng, and new martial arts schools opened near the temple. A film changed a real place.

words.d: a type of film or book with familiar settings and stories, such as westerns or martial arts films
a large Hong Kong film studio that made many martial arts films in the 1960s and 1970s

check.why: Shaw Brothers released The 36th Chamber of Shaolin in 1978.

lessons.title: Kung Fu on American Television
lessons.mainIdea: The ABC series Kung Fu (1972 to 1975) spread the English word widely and cast a white actor as its Chinese American hero.
reading: From 1972 to 1975, the ABC network aired a series called Kung Fu. Its hero was a Shaolin-trained monk of Chinese and white American parents. He wandered the American West in the 1800s. The show made the word kung fu familiar in millions of American homes.

The lead was played by David Carradine, a white actor. Many Asian American actors and viewers criticized the choice. They pointed out that Asian actors were rarely offered lead roles on American television. This practice of casting white actors in Asian roles is often called *whitewashing*.

The show was set in a real time: Chinese workers did help build the American West, including the Central Pacific Railroad in the 1860s. But its Shaolin scenes came from legend and the studio. It is evidence about 1970s television, not about Shaolin.

words.d: casting white actors to play characters of color, or leaving people of color out of a story
a television show that tells stories in many episodes over time

check.why: The ABC network aired Kung Fu from 1972 to 1975.

check.q: What is the show best evidence of?
check.why: The show tells historians about 1970s TV; its Shaolin scenes came from legend and the studio.

lessons.title: One Style, Many Spellings
lessons.mainIdea: Different spellings of one style's name, like Wing Chun, Ving Tsun and Wing Tsun, often mark different organizations.
reading: Chinese is written in characters, not letters. When a name is written in Latin letters, people must choose a spelling system. *Romanization* is the name for writing a language in the Latin alphabet. Cantonese and Mandarin also sound different.

One style can have many spellings. After Ip Man's death, his students' groups in Hong Kong and abroad used Wing Chun, Ving Tsun and Wing Tsun. The Ving Tsun Athletic Association was founded in Hong Kong in 1967 by Ip Man and his students. Some groups registered their spelling as a *trademark*.

A spelling can work like a family name. It can tell you which organization a school belongs to. So when a school sign uses a certain spelling, a historian asks which association uses it, and who gave that school's teacher the right to teach.

words.d: writing a language, such as Chinese, in the Latin alphabet
a name or symbol a group registers by law so others may not use it for the same service

lessons.title: Ranks on Paper: Duan Wei
lessons.mainIdea: In the late 1990s the Chinese Wushu Association created the duan wei system of written ranks for wushu.
reading: Older Chinese arts did not use colored belts. A student's place came from the teacher and the lineage. Belts and dan grades came from Japanese judo, where Kanō Jigorō began them in the 1880s.

In the late 1990s the Chinese Wushu Association launched the *duan wei* system. Duan means level and wei means rank. It has nine levels in three groups, marked on certificates. The goal was one national standard across many styles.

A *certificate* is a written record that an official body gives to a person. It names the holder, the rank and who awarded it. A historian can check a certificate against the body that issued it. A movie can give a hero a title, but it cannot issue a real rank.

words.d: the nine-level written rank system the Chinese Wushu Association created for wushu
a written record from an official body that names a person and what they earned

check.why: Duan wei has nine levels, arranged in three groups.

lessons.title: Films as Evidence of Their Time
lessons.mainIdea: Martial arts films are strong evidence about the years and places that made them, even when their stories are invented.
reading: A film is a *primary source* for the time it was made. Fist of Fury shows what Hong Kong filmmakers in 1972 wanted to say about foreign power in China. The Kung Fu series shows who American television cast in 1972.

Later films show later times. Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, directed by Ang Lee, won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film in 2001. It was made by companies in Taiwan, Hong Kong, mainland China and the United States. Its partners show how the film business had become global.

Kung Fu Panda, an American animated film from DreamWorks in 2008, set a cartoon story in an imagined China. Each film tells us about its makers and audiences. None of them is a record of how a real school was founded or who taught whom.

words.d: a document or object made at the time being studied
an American film prize, also called the Oscar, given each year since 1929

lessons.title: Chinese Schools Abroad
lessons.mainIdea: Chinese emigrants carried martial arts to cities abroad, where schools and lion dance troupes served their communities.
reading: From the 1800s, many Chinese people left southern China for Southeast Asia, the Americas and Australia. Many came from Guangdong. A community living far from its homeland is called a *diaspora*.

In many Chinatowns, martial arts schools were tied to family and district associations. These schools often trained *lion dance* troupes, which perform at Lunar New Year, weddings and store openings. The lion dance carries meanings of good fortune in many Chinese communities.

After 1965, the United States changed its immigration law. The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 ended quotas based on national origin. More Chinese immigrants arrived, and more schools opened. Many of them taught southern styles and used Cantonese names.

words.d: a community living far from its homeland, and keeping ties to it
a Chinese performance with a costumed lion, often by martial arts school troupes at festivals

look.title: A 1965 Law

look.prompt: How might a change in immigration law change the martial arts schools in an American city?

check.q: What did the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 end?
check.why: The 1965 act ended quotas based on national origin, and more Chinese immigrants arrived.

lessons.title: Questions for Any School Name
lessons.mainIdea: To check a school's name, historians ask for the place, the teacher line, the governing body and the documents.
reading: A school's name is a *claim*. It says where the art came from and who taught it. A historian checks a claim against records, the same way a detective checks a story against evidence.

Useful records include a charter or founding papers, certificates, photographs with dates, newspaper reports and letters. A charter is a document that creates an organization and states its purpose. Jingwu's founding in 1910 and the Ving Tsun Athletic Association's in 1967 are both on record.

Films, posters and legends are records too, but of something else. They show what people believed or enjoyed. When a film and a charter disagree about a school, the charter usually tells us more about the school, and the film tells us more about its audience.

words.d: a statement that something is true, which can be checked against evidence
a document that creates an organization and states its purpose
